relationship_summary: Brutus led the conspiracy that assassinated Caesar in 44 BCE. Earlier, Caesar had pardoned Brutus after Pharsalus and favored him with appointments. The rumor that Brutus was Caesar's biological son (via Servilia) is unverifiable.
Co-leader of the conspiracy against Caesar and co-commander of the Republican forces at Philippi. Cassius was Brutus' brother-in-law (married to Brutus' half-sister Junia Tertia).
Cato the Younger was Brutus' uncle (Servilia's half-brother). Brutus admired Cato as a philosophical and political exemplar, married Cato's daughter Porcia, and wrote a (lost) work in praise of Cato.
Daughter of Cato the Younger and wife of Brutus. Ancient sources portray her as a woman of Stoic fortitude who was aware of the conspiracy. She died (possibly by suicide) after Brutus' death.
Cicero was a philosophical mentor and political ally. Cicero dedicated several works to Brutus and they exchanged letters. Their political strategies diverged after the assassination.
Antony was Brutus' political adversary after Caesar's death. Antony's funeral oration turned public opinion against the conspirators, and he later defeated Brutus at Philippi.
Mother of Brutus. Servilia was Caesar's long-time mistress, which complicated Brutus' relationship with Caesar. She was politically active after the assassination.
Octavian was one of the triumvirs who opposed and defeated Brutus at Philippi. Octavian was Caesar's adopted heir, placing him in direct opposition to the assassins.
